newsitem.title: USA: U.S. may retaliate for envoy's expulsion from Belarus.
newsitem.headline: U.S. may retaliate for envoy's expulsion from Belarus.

text.p: The United States said on Monday that it may retaliate against Belarus for what it considers the unwarranted and unjustifiable arrest and expulsion of an American diplomat.
"We are studying our options," acting State Department spokesman John Dinger told reporters, adding that one of those options "is to reciprocate."
Serzh Alexandrov, a first secretary at the U.S. Embassy, was arrested at a protest against President Alexander Lukashenko's policies on Sunday and told to leave the country.
Dinger said the diplomat would comply with the order but he called the charges against Alexandrov "simply false."

The incident underscores the deteriorating ties between Belarus and the United States. On Friday, the State Department announced that it had cut off $40 million in aid to Belarus due to that country's human rights performance.

Dinger said Alexandrov was detained despite having clearly identified himself as a diplomat. "He was not immediately released despite the intervention of other U.S. diplomats present at the scene. And he was not shown the respect due an official representative of the United States Department of State."
"All of these actions constitute serious violations of normal diplomatic practice," the spokesman said.

He added that it was not unusual in the course of covering events such as Sunday's that U.S. diplomats would be caught up when there was a security cordon. "(But) it is extremely unusual for American diplomats not to be very quickly released once they identify themselves to authorities."
The U.S. ambassador to Belarus, Kenneth Yalovitz, immediately protested to Minsk over the expulsion, and similar complaints were lodged with the Belarus Embassy in Washington, Dinger said.

"We view this matter with the utmost seriousness and gravity ... This action marks a further step in the movement by the government of Belarus away from democratic reforms and respect for human rights.," he said.
He insisted that Alexandrov was carrying out normal duties, but a Belarus state television news reader said he had been working as a spy for the Central Intelligence Agency.

The United States has been one of the most vociferous critics of Lukashenko's increasingly authoritarian rule and protested when the local executive director of the Soros Foundation, Peter Bern, was barred from the country recently.
Bern, accused of supporting the opposition, is also a U.S. citizen and, like Alexandrov, attended an unsanctioned rally.
